extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for identifying, analyzing, and resolving statutory and nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting issues during patent examination, including tests, evidentiary limits, procedural fixes (e.g., terminal disclaimers), and special rules (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 121/consonance, filing-date priority).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory double patenting (35 U.S.C. § 101) — same invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on 35 U.S.C. § 101 — an applicant (or assignee) is prohibited from obtaining two patents for the same invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliable test: Is there an embodiment that falls within the scope of one claim, but not the other? Could one claim be literally infringed without literally infringing the other claim? If the answer is 'yes' to either question, then there is no basis for a statutory double patenting rejection. Statutory (35 U.S.C. 101) double patenting requires that the examined claim and the claim of the potentially conflicting patent/application exactly match in scope. Note: A terminal disclaimer (TD) will NOT overcome a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory double patenting (obviousness-type, ODP)
rubrics_metrics.description: A judicially created doctrine prohibiting issuance of a patent on an invention that is an obvious variation of an invention for which the applicant (or assignee) already has a patent (unless conditions such as a terminal disclaimer are met).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat ODP analogously to a 35 U.S.C. § 103 analysis: determine the scope and content of the 'Prior Art', ascertain the differences between the 'Prior Art' and the claim at issue, resolve the level of ordinary skill in the art, and evaluate evidence of secondary considerations. Nonstatutory DP is NOT a prior art rejection — the patent or co-pending application used in the analysis does not need to qualify as prior art, but any secondary references used in the obviousness analysis should qualify as prior art within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. § 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose information material to patentability (Duty of Candor, 37 C.F.R. § 1.56)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must disclose relevant unpublished USPTO applications, published applications, and patents to inform the examiner of potential double-patenting references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible DP situations to disclose include: applications filed by the same inventive entity, filed by different inventive entities having a common joint inventor, filed by at least one applicant in common who is not a common joint inventor (AIA cases), filed by a common assignee, or filed by different assignees but subject to a joint research agreement (CREATE Act or 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) / 102(c)). Applicant must provide a copy of each cited pending unpublished U.S. application per 37 C.F.R. § 1.98(a)(2)(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the claims — claims are primary for DP analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims of the potentially conflicting patent or application versus the examined claims are the basis for consideration in double patenting analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of the specification of the potentially conflicting patent or application is generally prohibited except for limited exceptions (e.g., claim term definitions, support). The examiner should compare claim scopes first and resort to specification only where permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper/limited uses of specification (MPEP § 804 II(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification can be used in certain circumstances to aid DP analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted uses include: using the specification as a dictionary for claim terminology; using portions of the disclosure which provide support for the claims in the potentially conflicting patent or application to determine whether claim sets represent an obvious variation. See MPEP 804 II(b)(1) for scope of allowable uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawn claims in copending cases — when to consider
rubrics_metrics.description: Withdrawn claims in copending applications have specific treatment in provisional NSDP analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Withdrawn claims in a reference (copending) application must be considered in a provisional nonstatutory double patenting (NSDP) analysis of elected claims in an application under examination. However, withdrawn claims in the case under examination should never be considered in a NSDP rejection of that case.

rubrics_metrics.name: A 35 U.S.C. § 101 DP rejection requires exact same scope
rubrics_metrics.description: For a statutory double patenting rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 101, the two claims must exactly match in scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examined claim and the claim of the potentially conflicting patent/application do not exactly match in scope, do not make a statutory (35 U.S.C. 101) double patenting rejection; perform further analysis for possible nonstatutory double patenting instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer cannot overcome statutory (35 U.S.C. § 101) DP
rubrics_metrics.description: A terminal disclaimer is ineffective to overcome a statutory double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory language of 35 U.S.C. § 101 establishes that the same invention cannot be patented twice; therefore a TD is not an appropriate remedy for true 'same invention' rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonstatutory DP: examples where method claims render product obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Method claims can make a product claim an obvious variation for ODP purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: An issued patent claims a method requiring a compound (Formula I) for preparing a product. A later application claims the compound itself. Because the compound is required to practice the issued method claim, the method of the issued patent may be used to reject the compound claim under nonstatutory double patenting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical ways to overcome nonstatutory DP rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Available applicant responses to a provisional/proper NSDP rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include: amend claims to encompass non-obvious subject matter; provide persuasive arguments why the current claims are not obvious variants over the co-pending application/patent claims; file an appropriate terminal disclaimer pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 253 (to disclaim the terminal portion of a patent term); or abandon one of the cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: DP depends on filing date, not issue date
rubrics_metrics.description: Determinations and procedural requirements for DP (e.g., which application must file TD) are tied to effective filing dates rather than patent issue dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typically a terminal disclaimer is required in the later-filed case (see MPEP 1490(VI)(D)). Provisional ODP rejections should be managed based on which application is earlier-filed: if the provisional ODP rejection is the only rejection remaining in the earlier-filed application, it should be withdrawn to permit the earlier-filed application to issue without a TD; if it's the only rejection remaining in the later-filed application, a TD must be required before withdrawing the provisional ODP rejection. Note: A later-issued patent may nonetheless invalidate an earlier-issued patent under nonstatutory DP (e.g., Gilead v. Natco).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two terminal disclaimers needed for same-day filings
rubrics_metrics.description: When two or more applications are filed on the same day and claim obvious variations of each other, TD treatment differs from ordinary earlier/later rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To overcome provisional NSDP rejections when both applications are filed on the same day, the provisional NSDP rejection made in each application should be maintained until a showing is made that the claims are patentably distinct or a terminal disclaimer is filed in both applications. See MPEP 1490 and the 'n-1' rule discussion; earlier-filed determination takes into account certain benefit claims (35 U.S.C. 120, 121, 365(c)) but not provisional or foreign priority under 35 U.S.C. 119(e) / 119(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Helpful reminders for terminal disclaimers — formal requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Common reasons for terminal disclaimer disapproval and formalities required for an effective TD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common defects include: TD identifies a party who is not the applicant (applies to applications filed on or after 9/16/2012) — the signer must be identified as the applicant in the Application Data Sheet (ADS); TD does not include the 'enforceable only during the period of common ownership' clause required by 37 C.F.R. § 1.321(c); TD does not state the extent of ownership/interest of the person who signed or the extent of the organization's ownership interest on whose behalf the person signed (37 C.F.R. § 1.321(b)(3)). Resubmission should include a corrected/replacement TD.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP/Basell: use of specifications to interpret claims and determine obvious variants
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification of the earlier (or later) patent/application may be used to learn the meaning of terms, interpret the coverage of a claim, and determine whether claims are obvious variants (In re Basell; MPEP § 804 II(B)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if later claims are narrower species of earlier claims, if the species were disclosed in the earlier specification such that the species fall within the meaning of the earlier claims, a nonstatutory DP rejection can be proper. Use specifications only for permitted purposes (term meaning, claim coverage, support for obvious_variation analysis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification disclosure of utility can create ODP (Sun Pharmaceutical v. Eli Lilly)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that discloses an unclaimed use of a compound can render later claims to that use invalid for obviousness-type double patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Earlier patent disclosed using gemcitabine to fight cancer (but did not claim it); later patent claimed methods of using gemcitabine to treat cancer — later claims were held invalid for ODP because the later claims simply claimed a use disclosed in the earlier specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 121 safe harbor and requirement to maintain consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: The third sentence of 35 U.S.C. 121 provides a safe harbor from double patenting for applications filed as a result of a restriction requirement, but specific conditions apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To invoke the § 121 safe harbor, consonance with the original restriction requirement must be maintained (including species elections). MPEP § 804.01 emphasizes the Office's burden to guard against erroneous restrictions that could improperly produce multiple patents. Failure to maintain consonance can forfeit the § 121 protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: When 35 U.S.C. 121 prohibition does NOT apply
rubrics_metrics.description: Situations where the § 121 safe harbor against using a related patent/application as a reference does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Two or more applications filed with no restriction requirement made (i.e., voluntary divisional); claims amended so they are not commensurate with the restriction requirement (consonance not maintained); restriction withdrawn (rejoinder); restriction/lack of unity only made in a PCT application; claims are directed to identical subject matter. In these cases § 121's protection may not be available.

rubrics_metrics.name: ODP-Anticipation: examined claim fully encompassed by potentially conflicting claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A category of nonstatutory double patenting where the examined claim is generic to (fully encompassed by) a claim in the potentially conflicting patent or application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the examined claims are fully encompassed by a claim in the potentially conflicting patent/application, an ODP-anticipation rejection is appropriate and no Graham v. Deere (full obviousness) analysis is needed. Visualize via claim-inclusion Venn diagram: if the examined claim lies entirely within the scope of the conflicting claim, treat as anticipation for ODP purposes.
